div.head: Að 1
div.ab: Twelfhyndes mannes að forstent VI ceorla aþ; forðam, gif man þone twelfhyndan man wrecan sceolde, he bið fullwrecen on syx ceorlan, 7 his wergyld bið VI ceorla wergyld.
Be Mirciscan aðe. Twelf-hendes mannes að forstent VI ceorla að; forðam, gif man þone twelfhendan man wrecan scolde, he bið fulwrecen on six ceorlan, 7 his wergild bið six ceorla wergild.

(De weregildo tƿelfhindes.) Tƿelfhyndes hominis iusiurandum contraualet sex uillanorum iusiurandum; quia, si tƿelfhynde man (-dus homo) uindicari deberet, plene uindicaretur in VI ceorlis, et eius weregildum est VI ceorlorum weregildum.

Concerning the Mercian oath The oath of a man of a 1200 wergild is equivalent to the oath of six ceorls; for, if a man of 1200 wergild is to be avenged, he is fully avenged on six ceorls, and his wergild is the wergild of six ceorls.

Concerning the Mercian Oath. The oath of a man with a wergild of twelve hundred shillings equals the oath of six laymen: therefore, if a man with a wergild of twelve hundred shillings must be avenged, he will be fully avenged on six laymen; furthermore, his wergild will be the wergilds of six laymen.

(Vom Mercischen Eide D; Vom Mercier-Recht falsch O). Der Eid eines 1200 [Schilling-]Mannes vertritt an Werth den Eid 6 Gemeinfreier; denn wenn man den 1200 [Schilling-]Mann rächen müsste, so ist er voll gerächt in [Erschlagung von] 6 Gemeinfreien, und sein Wergeld ist das Wergeld (-der Ld) von 6 Gemeinfreien.

(Of the Mercian oath, D; Of Mercian law, wrongly, O). The oath of a twelve-hundred [shilling] man is worth the oath of 6 ceorls; for if one had to avenge the twelve-hundred man, he is fully avenged in [the slaying of] 6 ceorls, and his wergild is the wergild (wergilds, Ld) of 6 ceorls.
div.note: Liebermann prints D (Cambridge, Corpus Christi College 201, f. 102, after Mirce, c. 1060), O (Cambridge, Corpus Christi College 190, p. 418, after Mirce, c. 1070) and H (Textus Roffensis f. 39v, after Swerian, c. 1120), with Ld, the Quadripartitus and the Instituta Cnuti III 44–45. K is H; D is also given here. H puts clause 2 before 1. Liebermann dates Að c. 950–c. 1050. D's restriction to Mercia contradicts clause 2 and is perhaps not original, introduced by the compiler because he found the piece after Mirce. In H the ‘1’ of ‘twelfhyndan’ is on an erasure and ‘man’ is written above. In H, Mirce follows after a paragraph break. Clause number 1 added. Liebermann compares Mirce 1.1.
